title: Structured Logging & Metrics
objectives: Emit structured JSON logs with levels and request IDs instead of parsed prose
Propagate a correlation/request ID across services and into responses
Choose the right small metric set (RED/USE) and keep cardinality bounded
Classify telemetry events as logs vs metrics and reject metric labels that explode cardinality
body:
At 03:00 the pager fires. You grep the logs and find four thousand lines that all say 'Error: something went wrong'. Nothing is knowable. Observability is the practice of instrumenting software so that 03:00-you can answer questions the code never anticipated — and it starts with two primitive types: logs and metrics.

## The problem

Free-text logs are for humans of a specific moment; they cannot be queried, joined or correlated. Ad-hoc metrics ('count everything!') die of cardinality: a metric with a user-ID label creates one time series per user, and the monitoring system falls over. Constraints: queryable at 03:00, joinable across services, cheap enough to keep forever.

## Structured logs

One event, one JSON object:

```json
{"ts":"2026-09-12T09:14:03.221Z","level":"error","msg":"db query failed","requestId":"req-a1","route":"POST /checkout","err":"ETIMEDOUT","durationMs":5003}
```

Now `jq 'select(.level=="error" and .durationMs>1000)'` works, fields are typed, and the line joins to traces by requestId. Levels are a severity contract, not adjectives:

- **debug** — developer detail; off in production (or sampled)
- **info** — business events: request handled, order placed, job done
- **warn** — degraded but functioning: retries, slow queries, fallback engaged
- **error** — this operation failed and needs attention
- **fatal** — the process is exiting

Log in the language of intent, not implementation: 'checkout failed: payment declined' beats 'NullPointerException at line 402' — carry the stack trace in a field, not as the message.

## Correlation and request IDs

The thread tying logs together across services: middleware assigns (or trusts upstream's) x-request-id, attaches it to a context, and every log line of that request carries it. Echo it in the error response so a user's support ticket contains the exact search key. One grep/label-filter later, the full journey of one request is on screen instead of a interleaved pile of other people's requests.

## Metrics: small, bounded, eager

Metrics are pre-aggregated numbers cheap to store and alert on — the opposite tradeoff from logs. Two standard sets:

- **RED** (request-driven services): Rate, Errors, Duration per endpoint.
- **USE** (resources): Utilization, Saturation, Errors for CPU, disk, DB pool, queues.

Cardinality is the constraint that decides everything. Labels like route ('/users/:id') and status_code ('500') are bounded — dozens of series. Labels like user_id, order_id, or full URL with query string explode into unbounded series; they belong in logs and traces, never in metric labels. Decide the label set when writing the metric; there is no deleting a high-cardinality series cheaply after a week in production.

## The split

Logs answer 'what exactly happened in this request'; metrics answer 'how is the system doing overall, and when did it change'. The flow that works: a metric (p95 latency of /checkout) pages you; correlation ID narrows the time window; logs with that ID reconstruct the failure; a trace (next lesson) shows which hop broke. Alert on metrics, investigate with logs and traces.

## Best practices

- One JSON object per log line; never multi-line stack traces in the message field.
- Log at the boundary where something was decided (handler, client call), not in every function.
- Attach requestId, route, user role (not PII like email) to every line via context.
- RED for services, USE for resources; add metrics only when something will alert or graph them.
- Debug logs sampled or level-gated in production; volume is a cost.

## Common mistakes

- String levels ('warn') vs numeric mixed with text — pick one encoding.
- Logging PII (emails, tokens, card numbers) into systems with 30-day-to-forever retention.
- Metric labels with unbounded values (user_id, raw URLs) — cardinality bankruptcy.
- alerting on logs ('grep ERROR > 0') — logs are for investigation, metrics for alerting.
- Catch-block logging with no context fields — an error nobody can correlate.

exercise.prompt: Write a telemetry linter in JavaScript. lintEvent(event) returns { level, issues } for one emitted event: level 'log' or 'metric'; a log event is INVALID if it lacks requestId or carries PII-looking fields (email, token, card); a metric is INVALID if any label value is unbounded-looking (ids, raw urls, emails) or the name is not snake_case. Render the lint report for the sample events.
hints: PII-shaped keys: email, token, card. Check the keys of the fields object.
Unbounded label keys: anything containing 'id' or 'url' — route and status are fine.
snake_case test: /^[a-z]+(_[a-z0-9]+)*$/ on the metric name.

questions.prompt: Why do microservices echo the same x-request-id downstream instead of generating a new one per hop?
options: One ID ties together every log line and trace span of the request across all services
questions.explanation: A shared correlation ID is the join key: one filter (or trace view) reconstructs the whole request journey instead of one service's fragment.

questions.prompt: Which metric is safe from a cardinality perspective?
questions.explanation: route and status have bounded value sets (dozens of series). user_id, full SQL text and raw URLs are unbounded — they belong in logs/traces, not metric labels.

questions.prompt: Your service uses a queue that is filling up faster than it drains. Which USE metric points at the problem most directly?
questions.explanation: USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors. A growing queue depth is saturation: the resource has more work arriving than capacity to drain it.
